p.src: Now the Great Sage Sun, together with Bajie and Sha Monk, went out from the city wall to meet them head-on. They saw that the demons were all lions of assorted coats: the Yellow Lion Demon led the way; the Suanni Lion and Elephant-Seizing Lion were on the left; the Baize Lion and Raccoon-Subduing Lion were on the right; the Macaque Lion and Snow Lion brought up the rear; and in their midst stood a nine-headed lion. The blue-faced monster carried a precious brocade banner embroidered with clustered flowers and stayed close beside the nine-headed lion; Cunning Eccentric and Eccentric Cunning bore two red banners. Together they formed ranks in the northern quarter.

p.src: Bajie, rash as ever, strode forward and cursed, “You thieving monster who stole our treasures! Why have you gathered these balls of fur and brought them here?” The Yellow Lion Demon gnashed his teeth and cursed, “You vicious bald scoundrel! Yesterday, three of you fought me alone. I withdrew in defeat and let you have your way, yet how could you be so cruel as to burn my cave, ruin my mountain grounds, and harm my kin? The hatred between us is as deep as the sea. Do not flee—take a blow from your lord’s spade!” Gallant Bajie raised his rake and met the blow. They had only just crossed weapons, with neither yet gaining the upper hand, when the Macaque Lion Demon swung an iron caltrop club and the Snow Lion Demon wielded a three-edged mace, charging straight in to strike. Bajie shouted, “Well come!” On this side, Sha Monk swiftly drew his demon-subduing staff and stepped forward to help. Then the Suanni and Baize demons, together with the Elephant-Seizing and Raccoon-Subduing demons, surged forward as one. Here the Great Sage Sun held the whole band of demons at bay with his gold-banded cudgel. The Suanni wielded a heavy cudgel, the Baize copper hammers, the Elephant-Seizer a steel spear, and the Raccoon-Subduer a battle-axe. Those seven lion demons against these three fierce monks—what a battle it was:

p.src: Cudgel, hammer, spear, axe, and three-edged mace; caltrop club, knobbed club, and four-pointed spade. Seven lions with seven keen-edged arms surrounded three monks, all shouting battle cries. The Great Sage’s gold-banded iron cudgel was fearsome; Sha Monk’s precious staff was seldom matched in the mortal world. Bajie raged like a gale, displaying his might; his nine-toothed rake flashed with a baleful gleam. Blocking before and guarding behind, each showed his skill; parrying left and meeting right, all fought bravely. From the city wall the princes raised their spirits, beating drums and clashing gongs to give them courage. Darting in and snatching away, they displayed their magic, fighting till heaven and earth grew dark and seemed overturned.

p.src: The band of demons fought the Great Sage and his two companions for half a day, until evening fell unnoticed. Bajie’s mouth streamed with sticky drool, and his legs were growing weak. He made a feint with his rake and fled from the field. The Snow Lion and Macaque Lion demons shouted after him, “Where do you think you are going? Take this!” The fool could not dodge in time. One of them struck him squarely across the spine with the mace, and he collapsed to the ground, crying only, “I’m done for! I’m done for!” The two demons seized Bajie by the bristles and tail, carried him before the nine-headed lion, and reported, “Grand Sire, we have captured one of them.”

p.src: Before they had finished speaking, Sha Monk and Pilgrim too were driven back, and all the demons came rushing after them. Pilgrim plucked out a handful of hairs, chewed them to pieces, and spat them forth, crying, “Transform!” At once they became over a hundred little Pilgrims, who swarmed around and enclosed the Baize, Suanni, Elephant-Seizing, Raccoon-Subduing, and Golden-Haired Lion demons in their midst. Sha Monk and Pilgrim then pressed forward again and struck from all sides. By nightfall they had captured the Suanni and Baize, though the Raccoon-Subduing and Elephant-Seizing demons escaped. The Golden-Haired Lion reported the news to the old monster. When the old monster learned that two lions had been lost, he ordered, “Bind Zhu Bajie, but do not harm his life. When he returns my two lions, we shall give Bajie back to him; but if he acts foolishly and kills my two lions, we shall kill Bajie to pay for their lives.” That night the demons rested outside the city, of which no more need be said.

p.src: Now the Great Sage Sun carried the two lion demons close to the city. When the old king saw them, he immediately ordered the gate opened and sent twenty or thirty officers out with ropes. They bound the lion demons and carried them into the city. The Great Sage Sun recalled his magic hairs and went straight up the city tower with Sha Monk to see Tripitaka. Tripitaka said, “That battle was perilous indeed. I wonder whether Wuneng is still alive?” Pilgrim replied, “He is fine. We have captured these two demons, so those creatures will certainly not dare hurt him. For now, bind these two securely. Tomorrow morning we shall exchange them for Bajie.” The three young princes kowtowed to Pilgrim and said, “Master, when you first fought, we saw only one of you; but after you feigned defeat and withdrew, how did there suddenly come to be over a hundred copies of your body? And when you approached the city after capturing the demons, you were one again. What manner of magic is this?” Pilgrim laughed and said, “I have eighty-four thousand hairs upon my body. Each one can become ten, each ten a hundred; transformations numbering hundreds, thousands, millions, and billions are all produced by the art of bodies beyond the body.” The princes each prostrated themselves in reverence. A vegetarian meal was served at once, and they ate it there upon the city tower. At every battlement they set out lanterns and banners, wooden clappers, bells, gongs, and drums; the watches were assigned and tally-arrows passed along, while cannon blasts and shouts rang out.

Meanwhile, I shall secretly fly over the city and seize their master, together with the old king and his sons. I will return first to Nine-Bend Coiling Cave and await your victorious report.” The Yellow Lion accepted the plan and led the Macaque Lion, Snow Lion, Elephant-Seizing Lion, and Raccoon-Subduing Lion to the city, each bearing his weapon. Whipping up wind and brewing fog, they challenged their foes to battle. Here Pilgrim and Sha Monk leapt from the city wall and cursed in ringing voices, “You vile thieving monsters! Return our junior brother Bajie at once, and we shall spare your lives; otherwise, every one of you shall have his bones ground and body smashed to pieces!” The demons would hear none of it and surged forward together. The Great Sage and his brother each employed his cunning and held off the five lions. This battle was very different from the one the day before:

p.src: While the five motley-coated lion demons were fighting Pilgrim and Sha Monk at the height of the fray, the old monster rode a black cloud straight up to the city tower. He shook his head, terrifying all the civil and military officials, high and low, as well as the men guarding the city, so badly that they tumbled down from the wall. He rushed into the tower, opened his mouths, and carried Tripitaka, the old king, and his sons out in a single sweep; then he returned to the ground in the northern quarter and took Bajie into another of his mouths. For each of his nine heads had a mouth of its own. One mouth held Tang Monk, one held Bajie, one held the old king, one held the eldest prince, one held the second prince, and one held the third prince. Six mouths held six people, leaving three mouths empty. He cried aloud, “I am going on ahead!” When the five lesser lion demons saw that their grandsire had triumphed, each displayed still greater prowess.

p.src: When Pilgrim heard the people shouting from the city walls, he knew they had fallen into the enemy's trap and quickly warned Sha Monk to be on his guard. He then plucked every hair from his arms, chewed them to pieces in his mouth, and blew them out, transforming them into hundreds upon hundreds of little Pilgrims, who surged forward in a single host. They promptly dragged down the Macaque Lion, captured the Snow Lion alive, seized the Elephant-Grappling Lion, overturned the Leopard-Subduing Lion, and beat the Yellow Lion to death, then swept noisily toward the prefectural city. Only the Blue-Faced One and the three monsters, Crafty Freak and his two fellows, managed to turn and escape. When the officials on the walls saw this, they opened the gates once more, bound the five lion spirits with ropes, and carried them into the city. Before any judgment could be passed, the queen came weeping and bowed to Pilgrim, saying, “Divine Master, my lord, his sons, and your master are surely doomed. What is to become of this isolated city?” The Great Sage recalled his magic hairs and bowed to the queen. “Worthy queen, do not grieve. It is only because I captured his seven lion spirits that the old fiend used his snatching magic and carried off my master, your lord, and his sons. I am certain they have suffered no harm. At first light tomorrow, we two brothers will go into the mountain. We shall assuredly capture the old fiend and restore all four princes to you.” Hearing this, the queen and all the court ladies bowed to Pilgrim and said, “May our lord and his sons return alive, and may the royal realm stand secure.” After bowing, they returned to the palace one by one, their eyes full of tears. Pilgrim instructed the officials, “Skin the Yellow Lion spirit that was beaten to death; and bind and chain the six living lion spirits securely. Bring us some vegetarian food, so that we may eat and sleep. Set your minds at ease; I shall see that no harm comes to you.”

p.src: As the two of them stood admiring the scenery from the mountaintop, they suddenly saw the Blue-Faced One emerge from among the cliffs and ravines, a short cudgel in his hand. Pilgrim shouted, “Where do you think you're going? Old Sun is here!” The little fiend was so frightened that he went tumbling and scrambling down into the ravine. The two pursued him all the way, but then lost every trace of him. After advancing a few more paces and rounding a bend, they came upon a cave dwelling whose two mottled stone doors were tightly shut. A stone tablet was set crosswise above the lintel, engraved in regular script with ten large characters: “Bamboo Joint Mountain of Myriad Spirits, Nine-Bend Coiling Cave.”

p.src: The little fiend had in fact run into the cave and shut its doors behind him. He went to the inner chamber and reported to the old fiend, “Grandfather, two more monks have come outside.” The old fiend asked, “Have your king and the Macaque Lion, Snow Lion, Elephant-Grasper, and Leopard-Subduer returned?” “No, no,” replied the little fiend. “There were only two monks looking about from the high mountain peak. As soon as I saw them, I turned and ran. They came chasing after me, but I got inside and shut the doors.” Hearing this, the old fiend lowered his head and said nothing. After a long while, tears suddenly streamed down his face, and he cried, “What misery! My grandson Yellow Lion is dead, and my grandsons Macaque Lion and the others have all been captured by the monks and taken into the city. How can I ever avenge this wrong?” Bajie was bound nearby, huddled together with the king and his sons and the Tang Monk, all suffering in wretched fear. When he heard the old fiend say that all his grandsons had been captured by the monks and taken into the city, he rejoiced inwardly and said, “Master, do not be afraid; Your Highnesses, do not grieve. My elder brother has won the victory, captured all the fiends, and found his way here to rescue us.” No sooner had he finished than they heard the old fiend call out, “You little ones, guard this place well. I shall go out and seize those two monks, bring them in, and punish them all together.”

p.src: Look at him: wearing no armor and carrying no weapon, he strode boldly to the front, where he could already hear Sun Pilgrim shouting challenges. He flung the cave doors wide and, without saying a word, charged straight at Pilgrim. Pilgrim raised his iron staff to block the blow aimed at his head. Sha Monk swung his precious staff and struck. The old fiend shook his head; the eight heads on either side opened their mouths together and effortlessly seized Pilgrim and Sha Monk between their jaws, carrying them back into the cave. He ordered, “Bring ropes!” Crafty Freak, his fellow, and the Blue-Faced One—the three who had escaped with their lives the previous night—immediately brought two ropes and bound the pair fast. The old fiend demanded, “You impudent monkey, you captured seven of my sons and grandsons; now I have captured all four of you monks and four princes besides. That should be enough to repay the lives of my descendants. You little ones, choose some thorn switches and willow cudgels. Give this monkey a beating first, to avenge my grandson Yellow Lion.” Each of the three little fiends took up a willow cudgel and concentrated his blows on Pilgrim. But Pilgrim's body had been tempered in the crucible. Those puny willow sticks could do no more than scratch an itch for him. He uttered not a sound and paid no heed, however hard they thrashed him. At the sight, Bajie, the Tang Monk, and the princes were each chilled to the bone. Before long, the willow cudgels broke. They kept beating him until nightfall, striking more blows than anyone could count. Sha Monk, seeing how long Pilgrim had been beaten, could bear it no longer and said, “Let me take a hundred or so blows in his place.” The old fiend replied, “There is no need to hurry. Your beating begins tomorrow. We shall beat every one of you in turn.” Bajie grew anxious and said, “Then the day after tomorrow it will be Old Hog's turn!” After they had beaten him for another while, darkness gradually fell. The old fiend called out, “You little ones, stop for now. Light the lamps and eat something, while I go to Brocade Cloud Nest for a short sleep. Since all three of you have suffered at their hands, keep a careful watch and resume the beating tomorrow morning.” The three little fiends moved a lamp closer, then took their willow cudgels and struck Pilgrim on the crown as though beating a wooden watchman's clapper—tick-tock, tock-tick—several quick blows, then several slow ones. As the night deepened, however, they all began to doze.

p.src: Pilgrim used an escape spell, shrank his body, and slipped free of the ropes. He shook out his hairs and straightened his clothing. Taking the staff from his ear, he gave it a shake until it was as thick as a bucket and some twenty feet long, then addressed the three little fiends: “You wretched beasts have given your lord here a great many blows. Yet your lord remains just as he was. Now let your lord press this staff against you a little and see how you fare!” With one light press against each of the three little fiends, he flattened them into three cakes of flesh. He then trimmed the lamp until it burned brightly and untied Sha Monk. Bajie's bonds were so tight that he could bear them no longer, and he cried aloud, “Brother, my hands and feet are swollen from these ropes! Why didn't you free me first?” That one shout from the fool immediately awakened the old fiend. The old fiend sprang up with a roll and demanded, “Who has been set free?” Hearing him, Pilgrim blew out the lamp in one breath. With no time to attend to Sha Monk or the others, he wielded his iron staff, smashed through several doors, and escaped.

With one light press against each of the three little fiends, he flattened them into three cakes of flesh.
He then trimmed the lamp until it burned brightly and untied Sha Monk.
Bajie's bonds were so tight that he could bear them no longer, and he cried aloud, “Brother, my hands and feet are swollen from these ropes! Why didn't you free me first?”
That one shout from the fool immediately awakened the old fiend.
The old fiend sprang up with a roll and demanded, “Who has been set free?”
Hearing him, Pilgrim blew out the lamp in one breath. With no time to attend to Sha Monk or the others, he wielded his iron staff, smashed through several doors, and escaped.

p.src: The old fiend reached the central hall and called, “You little ones, why have the lights gone out? Surely none of the prisoners has escaped?” He called once, but no one answered; he called again, but still no one answered. When he fetched a light and looked, he saw three blood-soaked cakes of flesh on the floor. The old king and his sons, the Tang Monk, and Bajie were all still there; only Pilgrim and Sha Monk were missing. Lighting torches, he searched front and back and found Sha Monk still standing beneath the gallery with his back pressed against it. He seized him, threw him down, and bound him again as before. He searched again for Pilgrim, but saw that several successive doors had all been smashed. He knew then that Pilgrim had broken through them and escaped. He made no attempt to pursue him, but had the broken doors repaired where possible and boarded over elsewhere, then stayed to guard his domain. Of this we shall say no more.

p.src: Now Sun the Great Sage left the Nine-Bend Coiling Cave, mounted an auspicious cloud, and headed straight back to Yuhua Prefecture. There he saw the local earth gods from every quarter, together with the other deities and the City God, rise into the air to bow and welcome him. Pilgrim said, “Why have you only now come to see me tonight?” The City God replied, “We humble gods knew that the Great Sage had descended upon Yuhua Prefecture and was being hospitably detained by its worthy prince, so we did not dare present ourselves. Now that we know the prince and his people have encountered monsters and that the Great Sage has subdued them, we have come especially to pay our respects and welcome you.” Just as Pilgrim was angrily rebuking them, he saw the Golden-Headed Guardian and the divine generals of the Six Jia and Six Ding escorting an earth god. They knelt before him and said, “Great Sage, we have caught this local wretch and brought him here.” Pilgrim shouted, “Why are you making a commotion here instead of guarding my master at Bamboo-Knot Mountain?” The Ding and Jia gods replied, “Great Sage, after you escaped, that monster seized the Curtain-Lifting General again and tied him up as before. Seeing how immensely powerful he was, we escorted the earth god of Bamboo-Knot Mountain here. He knows the monster’s origins. We beg the Great Sage to question him; then you can decide how best to deal with the creature and rescue the holy monk and the worthy prince from their suffering.” Pilgrim was delighted to hear this. Trembling with fear, the earth god kowtowed and said, “That old monster descended upon Bamboo-Knot Mountain the year before last. The Nine-Bend Coiling Cave was originally the den of the six lions. Once the old monster arrived, all six acknowledged him as their grandsire. That grandsire is a nine-headed lion known as the Nine-Spirit Primordial Sage. To overcome him, you must go to the Palace of Wondrous Rock at the Eastern Pole and invite his master here; only then can he be subdued. No one else can hope to capture him.” Hearing this, Pilgrim pondered for some time before saying, “The Palace of Wondrous Rock at the Eastern Pole belongs to the Celestial Worthy Taiyi, Savior from Suffering—and his mount is indeed a nine-headed lion. So that is how it is.” He then ordered, “Guardians and Golden-Armored Gods, return with the earth god and secretly protect my master, my junior brothers, and the prefectural prince and his sons. The City God of this place shall guard the city.” Each of the gods obeyed and departed.

p.src: At the palace gate stood an immortal boy dressed in a rainbow cape. The moment he saw Sun the Great Sage, he went inside and announced, “Grand Master, the Great Sage Equaling Heaven who caused havoc in the Celestial Palace is outside.” On hearing this, the Celestial Worthy Taiyi, Savior from Suffering, immediately summoned the attendant immortals to welcome him. They escorted him into the palace, where he saw the Celestial Worthy seated aloft on a nine-colored lotus throne amid billions of rays of auspicious light. When the Celestial Worthy saw Pilgrim, he descended from his throne to greet him. Pilgrim bowed before him. Returning the courtesy, the Celestial Worthy said, “Great Sage, it has been several years since we last met. I heard some time ago that you had forsaken the Dao and turned to Buddhism, and were escorting the Tang Monk to the Western Heaven to fetch the scriptures. I suppose your meritorious mission is now complete?” Pilgrim replied, “My mission is not yet complete, though it is nearly so. But now, while escorting the Tang Monk through Yuhua Prefecture, we were received by the prince, who had his three sons take old Sun and my companions as masters to learn the martial arts. They had copies made of our three divine weapons, but unexpectedly thieves stole them during the night. When we searched for them at daybreak, we discovered that they had been stolen by a golden-haired lion spirit from Tiger-Mouth Cave on Leopard-Head Mountain north of the city. Old Sun recovered them by a stratagem, whereupon that spirit joined forces with several other lion spirits and fought a great battle with me. Among them was a nine-headed lion of immense supernatural power. He carried off my master, Bajie, the prince, and his three sons in his jaws and took them all to the Nine-Bend Coiling Cave on Bamboo-Knot Mountain. The next day, old Sun and Friar Sand went in pursuit, but we too were carried off in his jaws. Old Sun was bound and beaten countless times, but fortunately I used a transformation and escaped. The others are still suffering there. Only after questioning the local earth god did I learn that you, Celestial Worthy, are his master. I have therefore come especially to invite you to subdue him and rescue them.”

p.src: On hearing this, the Celestial Worthy immediately ordered an immortal general to go to the lion quarters, summon the lion keeper, and question him. The lion keeper was fast asleep and did not awaken until the generals shoved and shook him. They then seized him and hauled him into the central hall. The Celestial Worthy asked, “Where is the lion beast?” With tears streaming down his face, the servant kowtowed and cried only, “Spare my life! Spare my life!” The Celestial Worthy said, “Sun the Great Sage is here, so I shall not beat you for the moment. Tell me at once how your negligence allowed the nine-headed lion to escape.” The lion keeper replied, “Grand Master, the day before yesterday I saw a jar of wine in the Great-Thousand Sweet-Dew Hall. Foolishly, I stole it and drank it, then became so deeply intoxicated that I fell asleep. I failed to keep the beast tethered and locked, and that is how it escaped.” The Celestial Worthy said, “That wine was a gift from the Supreme Lord Laozi and is called the Jade Liquor of Reincarnation. After drinking it, you were bound to remain drunk and unconscious for three days. How many days has the lion beast been gone now?” The Great Sage replied, “According to the earth god, he descended there the year before last, so it has been two or three years by now.” The Celestial Worthy laughed and said, “That explains it, that explains it. A single day in the Celestial Palace is a year in the mortal world.” He told the lion keeper, “Rise for now. I spare you the death penalty. Come down to the mortal world with the Great Sage and me to recapture him. The rest of you immortals may all return; there is no need to follow us.”

A single roar from him reaches the Three Sages above and penetrates the Nine Springs below, yet ordinarily he does not lightly harm living creatures. Sun the Great Sage, go to his gate and challenge him to battle. Lure him outside so that I may recapture him.”

p.src: Hearing this, the Pilgrim at once drew his cudgel, leapt near the cave entrance, and shouted abuse: “You vile fiend, give our people back! You vile fiend, give our people back!” He called several times, but the old fiend was asleep and no one answered. Growing impatient, the Pilgrim swung his iron cudgel and fought his way inside, shouting and cursing without pause. Only then did the old fiend wake with a start. Furious, he scrambled up and roared, “After him! Fight!” He shook his head, opened his jaws, and lunged forward to seize him. The Pilgrim turned and leapt outside. The fiend pursued him outside, cursing, “Thieving monkey, where do you think you’re going?” Standing atop a high cliff, the Pilgrim laughed and said, “How dare you remain so insolent and brazen? You do not even know whether you are to live or die. Is that not your lord and master standing there?” As the fiend reached the foot of the cliff, the Celestial Worthy had already recited an incantation and called, “Yuansheng, my child, I have come.” Recognizing his master, the fiend dared not resist. He dropped all four paws to the ground and did nothing but kowtow. The lion keeper ran up from the side, seized its mane, and struck its neck with his fist a good hundred times, cursing, “You brute! Why did you run away and make me suffer for it?” The lion beast kept its mouth shut and dared neither speak nor move. Only when the lion keeper’s hand grew weary did he stop, and then he fitted a brocade saddlecloth upon the beast. The Celestial Worthy mounted it and commanded it to go. The beast sprang up onto a many-colored cloud and returned straight to Miaoyan Palace.

p.src: The Great Sage called his thanks toward the sky, then entered the cave. He first freed the King of Yuhua, next Tripitaka, and then Eight Rules, Friar Sand, and the three princes. Together they searched through the cave’s possessions and, proceeding at an easy pace, led everyone outside. Eight Rules gathered a quantity of dry firewood, piled it before and behind the cave, and set it alight, burning the winding Nine-Bend Cave into a blackened, ruined kiln. The Great Sage dismissed the assembled deities and ordered the local earth god to remain and guard the place. He then told Eight Rules and Friar Sand to use their magic and carry the king and his sons back to the prefecture. He himself supported the Tang Monk. Before long they reached the prefectural city. Evening was drawing on, and the royal consorts and officials all came out to receive them. A vegetarian banquet was laid out, and all sat down to enjoy it together. The elder and his disciples again rested in the Baosha Pavilion. The princes returned to the palace and each retired to his chamber. Nothing more occurred that night.

p.src: The next day the king issued another decree and held a grand vegetarian feast. Every official in the prefecture, high and low, came in turn to offer thanks. The Pilgrim also summoned butchers to kill the six living lions. They skinned them together with the yellow lion and prepared the meat for consumption. His Highness was delighted and immediately ordered them slaughtered: one was to be kept for the people within and outside the palace; one was to be divided among the chief secretary and other palace officials; the other five were chopped into pieces weighing one or two taels apiece, and commandants were sent to distribute them among the soldiers and civilians within and outside the city, so that everyone might eat a little—first to taste the flavor, and second to settle their fright. Every household looked upon the pilgrims with reverence.

p.src: Then the blacksmiths who had finished making the three kinds of weapons came before the Pilgrim, kowtowed, and said, “Grandfather, we humble craftsmen have finished the work.” He asked, “How much does each one weigh?” The blacksmiths replied, “The gold-banded cudgel weighs one thousand catties, while the nine-pronged rake and the demon-subduing staff each weigh eight hundred.” “That will do,” said the Pilgrim. He had the three princes summoned and told each to take up his weapon. The three sons said to the old king, “Royal Father, today our weapons are complete.” The old king said, “Because of these weapons, we father and sons nearly lost our lives.” The youngest prince said, “By good fortune our divine masters used their magic to rescue us, swept away the evil spirits, and removed all future danger. This is truly what is meant by calm seas and clear rivers—a world of perfect peace.” The old king and his sons then rewarded the craftsmen for their labor and went again to the Baosha Pavilion to bow in thanks for their masters’ instruction.

p.src: Tripitaka urged the Great Sage and the others to teach the martial arts quickly, lest they delay the journey. The three disciples each brandished his weapon and instructed the princes one by one in the palace courtyard. Within a few days the three princes had mastered all their exercises. They learned every one of the seventy-two methods governing advance and retreat, speed and restraint. This was partly because the princes were resolute and partly because the Great Sage Sun had earlier bestowed divine strength upon them. Thus they could all lift and wield the thousand-catty cudgel and the eight-hundred-catty rake and staff; compared with the martial arts they had practiced by themselves at first, the difference was truly as vast as heaven from the abyss. p.src: The princes again held a grand banquet to thank their masters for their instruction. They also brought out a large tray of gold and silver as a token of their gratitude. The Pilgrim laughed and said, “Take it back at once! Take it back! What use have we monks for such things?” Eight Rules said from the side, “We truly dare not accept gold or silver. But my robe was torn by those lion fiends, so if you would merely replace our clothes, that would be kindness enough.” The princes immediately summoned the tailors and, following the original colors and patterns, supplied several bolts each of blue, red, and tawny brocade, from which a robe was made for each of the three disciples. The three accepted them gladly, donned their brocade robes, prepared their baggage, and set out. Throughout the city and beyond its walls, old and young alike proclaimed them arhats descended to the mortal world and living Buddhas come down from heaven. The sound of drums and music and the brilliant colors of banners filled the streets and blocked the roads. Indeed, incense burned outside every household, and colored lanterns were offered before every gate. Only after escorting them a great distance did the people turn back, and the four pilgrims were at last able to leave the city and journey westward. Thus, having escaped the host of lions, they devoted themselves wholly to attaining the true fruit. Indeed:

u.src: The princes again held a grand banquet to thank their masters for their instruction.
They also brought out a large tray of gold and silver as a token of their gratitude.
The Pilgrim laughed and said, “Take it back at once! Take it back!
What use have we monks for such things?”
Eight Rules said from the side, “We truly dare not accept gold or silver. But my robe was torn by those lion fiends, so if you would merely replace our clothes, that would be kindness enough.”

The princes immediately summoned the tailors and, following the original colors and patterns, supplied several bolts each of blue, red, and tawny brocade, from which a robe was made for each of the three disciples.
The three accepted them gladly, donned their brocade robes, prepared their baggage, and set out.
